## Stimulus and pRF predict BOLD {role=concept time=3.5}

::: {.movie clip="stimulus_to_bold" height=4.5cm}
Simulated with prfmodel [-@prfmodel]: one pRF, one 300 s bar run. Not a measurement.
:::

::: notes
Line: a pRF model turns a stimulus into a predicted BOLD time course: overlap of bar and pRF, then the haemodynamic response.
Ask: before the cursor starts: when will the neural trace rise? (Each time the bar crosses the small circle at the upper right of fixation.)
Say: left, the visual field out to 8 degrees, with one voxel's pRF as a circle. Right, three rows on one time axis: the stimulus, a band per sweep with the bar's direction; the predicted neural response, the overlap of bar and pRF; and the predicted BOLD response, that overlap through the haemodynamic response. One cursor runs through the 300 s run. The neural trace rises at every crossing; the BOLD trace follows about 5 s later, smoother, with an undershoot in every blank. Both traces are predictions, nothing here is measured.
Status: [SIM] simulated with prfmodel (Gaussian 2D pRF at (2.5, 1.5) deg, sigma 1 deg, two-gamma HRF), clips/families/population_receptive_fields/stimulus_to_bold/data/run.csv; title drafted from the brief, for the lecturer to review.
:::

## A model is a chain of stages {role=concept time=3.5}

::: {.movie clip="model_as_chain" height=4.5cm}
Synthetic data: a predicted BOLD response, and the same plus noise. Not a measurement.
:::

::: notes
Line: the model in the modelling loop is a chain of stages, and the fitted parameters belong to particular stages.
Ask: which of the seven stages would you fit, and which would you fix? (The clip tags four: pooling, transformation, dynamics and the HRF.)
Say: the loop first: parameters and a stimulus feed a model, whose prediction is set against the data. Open the model and it is a chain: stimulus, features, spatial pooling, a transformation, neural dynamics, the haemodynamic response, BOLD. The dashed outline holds the five stages that are the model. The parameters theta sit on four of them. One pulse runs from the stimulus to BOLD, and the prediction is drawn over the data.
Status: [SIM] synthetic: the Gaussian pRF voxel's predicted BOLD for the first 150 s of the bar run, normalised to a peak of 1, and the same plus Gaussian noise (SD 0.12), clips/families/population_receptive_fields/model_as_chain/data/panel.csv; title drafted from the brief, for the lecturer to review.
:::

## Fits keep the best candidate {role=example time=4}

::: {.movie clip="grid_and_fit" height=4.5cm}
One measured voxel: 7t-aot-visual, sub-003 [@knapen2026aot], CC BY 4.0. The predictions are the model's.
:::

::: notes
Line: a pRF is fitted by trying candidate fields on a grid, keeping the one whose prediction matches the measurement best, then refining it.
Ask: after the four slow candidates: what tells you a candidate is better? (Its prediction lies on the measurement: a higher R squared.)
Say: left, the visual field out to 4 degrees; the candidate is a centre and a one-sigma circle. Right, the measured time course of one voxel and the candidate's prediction over it, with R squared. Four candidates slowly, then 48 quickly; the best so far stays as a dashed outline. The grid has 147 points: 7 by 7 centres from minus 3 to 3 degrees, sizes 0.5, 1 and 2. The best grid point is (2, 1) degrees, sigma 1, R squared 0.84. Refinement slides it in eleven steps to x 2.27, y 0.99, sigma 0.85, R squared 0.86.
Status: [DATA] the measured voxel is prfmodel's example dataset 7t-aot-visual, sub-003 (Knapen 2026, figshare, CC BY 4.0); the 64 candidates and their predictions were fitted with prfmodel, clips/families/population_receptive_fields/grid_and_fit/data/; title drafted from the brief, for the lecturer to review.
:::

## Independent fits make a map {role=concept time=4}

::: {.movie clip="fields_to_map" study="eccentricity end"}
690 simulated voxels, each fitted on its own with prfmodel [-@prfmodel]. Not measurements.
:::

::: notes
Line: a visual field map is not put in by the analysis: it appears when every voxel is fitted on its own and coloured by what its fit returned.
Ask: pause with Space on the complete eccentricity map (12.9 s). Coloured by the direction of each centre from fixation instead, which way will the bands run? (Across the first set: the bands now run the other way across the sheet.)
Say: left, the right half of the visual field; right, a sheet of cortex, one square per voxel. Each fit puts a dot at the fitted centre and colours the voxel's square by the centre's distance from fixation. No fit knows its neighbours, yet bands of colour form across the sheet: a map. Then every square and dot takes the colour of the centre's direction from fixation, and the bands run the other way. The voxels are simulated, on a model sheet of early visual cortex.
Status: [SIM] simulation of 690 voxels, each simulated with noise on a bar run and fitted on its own with prfmodel, clips/families/population_receptive_fields/fields_to_map/data/voxels.csv. The key-press hold at 12.9 s (stop eccentricity) is not on the slide yet: lecturekit 0.4.0 measures 0 frames of rest before it (README.md, log of 13 November 2026). Title drafted from the brief, for the lecturer to review.
:::
